claim: Letterman writes that in the Twelfth Corps, where the order reducing the medical transportation had not been carried out, a quoted report says it enabled the wounded to be removed from the field, sheltered, fed and dressed within six hours after the battle ended, and every capital operation to be performed within twenty-four hours after the wound was received.

source.edition: Medical Recollections of the Army of the Potomac, New York: D. Appleton and Company, 1866 (title page read)

quote: In the Twelfth Corps the order reducing the Medical transportation had not been carried out ... it enabled me to remove the wounded from the field, shelter, feed them, and dress their wounds, within six hours after the battle ended, and to have every capital operation performed within twenty-four hours after the wound was received.

data.name_period: removal, shelter, feeding and dressing within six hours; capital operations within twenty-four hours (Twelfth Corps)

value.text: within six hours after the battle ended; capital operations within twenty-four hours after the wound

scene.may_show: At the Twelfth Corps hospital, which kept its medical wagons, the wounded are brought in, sheltered, fed and dressed within six hours of the end of the fighting and the capital operations are done within twenty-four hours of the wound.

notes: one witness for one corps (McNulty, quoted by Letterman); the other corps' timings are gaps, never filled from this row

claim: Gross describes the field tourniquet: a stick of wood six inches long and a handkerchief or piece of roller with a thick compress.

source.edition: S. D. Gross, A Manual of Military Surgery, second edition, Philadelphia: J. B. Lippincott & Co., 1862 (entered 1861); clean OCR; the archive.org record dates it 1861

quote: every one may put into his pocket a stick of wood, six inches long, and a handkerchief or piece of roller, with a thick compress ... This simple contrivance, which has been instrumental in saving thousands of lives, constitutes what is called the field tourniquet.

data.name_period: field tourniquet (a stick, a handkerchief or roller, a thick compress)

scene.may_show: A soldier or surgeon checks bleeding from a limb with a handkerchief or roller knotted round it, a thick compress over the main artery and a six-inch stick turned to tighten it.

claim: The Park Service teachers' guide defines a dressing station as a makeshift area close to the battle where a medical officer gave first aid treatment.

source.edition: Care of the Wounded Student Program: Teachers' Guide (not stated)

quote: dressing station : makeshift area close to the battle where a medical officer gave first aid treatment.

data.relation: a makeshift area close to the battle where a medical officer gave first aid

notes: a glossary entry of a student guide without a printed source; the primary manuals (Tripler, Gross, the Steward's Manual) are to be read for the same point
